claim: FORCP (LINC00675) is one of the most significantly down-regulated lncRNAs in CRC tumors compared to normal tissue.
source: FORCP was one of the most significantly down-regulated lncRNAs in CRC tumors (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by microarray data from 83 CRC patient samples and 79 matched normal tissue shown in Figure 1A.

claim: FORCP is transcribed from chromosome 17 and is antisense to TMEM220-AS1.
source: FORCP is transcribed from chromosome 17 and is antisense to TMEM220-AS1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by genomic location data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: FORCP is expressed in a GI-tract-specific manner with high expression in normal human colon and stomach.
source: In normal human tissues, FORCP is expressed in a GI-tract-specific manner with high expression in the normal human colon and stomach (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from GTExPortal shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the colon, FORCP is approximately seven-fold less abundant than MALAT1 and three-fold less abundant than NORAD.
source: In addition, in the colon FORCP was ~seven- and three-fold less abundant than the highly expressed lncRNAs MALAT1 and NORAD, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by expression comparison data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: FORCP is almost exclusively expressed in well-differentiated CRC cell lines compared to poorly differentiated CRC cell lines (~4400 fold change).
source: However, in our RNA-seq from 7 CRC cell lines of which three were well-differentiated (C80, LS180, and SW1222) and four were poorly differentiated (HCT116, SW48, SW480, and RKO), FORCP was almost exclusively expressed in the well-differentiated CRC lines (~4400 fold change) (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from 7 CRC cell lines shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The annotated spliced FORCP transcript is approximately 1.5 kb long and has a canonical polyadenylation signal at its 3′ end.
source: The annotated spliced FORCP transcript is ~1.5 kb long and has a canonical polyadenylation signal at its 3′ end (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Northern blotting shows that FORCP runs at the expected size in SW1222 and LS180 and is undetectable in HCT116.
source: Northern blotting showed that FORCP runs at the expected size in SW1222 and LS180 and is undetectable in HCT116 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: FOXA1 is significantly more abundant at the mRNA level (~16 fold, p<0.0001) in well-differentiated CRC lines compared to poorly differentiated lines.
source: Among these, FOXA1 was the only transcription factor that was significantly more abundant at the mRNA (~16 fold, p<0.0001) and protein level in the well-differentiated lines as compared to the poorly differentiated lines (Figure 1D,E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: FOXA1 is significantly down-regulated in CRC tumors.
source: Additionally, FOXA1 was significantly down-regulated in CRC tumors (Figure 1F)
evidence: Supported by expression data from the UMMC cohort shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Knockdown of FOXA1 in LS180 and SW1222 significantly decreases FORCP levels.
source: knockdown of FOXA1 in LS180 and SW1222 significantly decreased FORCP levels (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and immunoblotting data after FOXA1 knockdown shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–E.

claim: FOXA1 binds to the FORCP locus as demonstrated by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR.
source: By performing FOXA1 ChIP-seq (Lazar et al., 2020) followed by ChIP-qPCR, we identified and validated FOXA1 binding to the FORCP locus (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by FOXA1 ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: FOXA1 enhances FORCP transcription in well-differentiated CRC cells.
source: These data suggest that FOXA1 enhances FORCP transcription in the well-differentiated CRC cells.
evidence: Inferred from FOXA1 binding to FORCP locus and decreased FORCP expression upon FOXA1 knockdown.

claim: FORCP is predominantly cytoplasmic, similar to GAPDH.
source: RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (RNA-FISH) and qRT-PCR from nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions suggested that FORCP is predominantly cytoplasmic, similar to GAPDH (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-FISH and qRT-PCR data from subcellular fractions shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: FORCP RNA has a positive maximum codon substitution frequency (CSF) score, similar to the protein-coding gene GAPDH but unlike the lncRNA NEAT1 which has a negative maxCSF score.
source: Next, using PhyloCSF, an algorithm that determines the probability of a multi-species nucleotide sequence alignment representing a protein-coding region, we found that FORCP RNA has a positive maximum codon substitution frequency (CSF), similar to the protein-coding gene GAPDH but unlike the lncRNA NEAT1 which had a negative maxCSF score (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by PhyloCSF analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: FORCP contains a short, 240 nt ORF that has the potential to be translated into a 79 amino acid small protein highly conserved between mammals.
source: Analysis of evolutionary conservation revealed a short, 240 nt ORF in FORCP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) that has the potential to be translated into a 79 amino acid small protein highly conserved between mammals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and conservation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Human FORCP and its mouse homolog (ENSMUSG00000085683.2/9130409J20Rik) are located at a syntenic region on human chromosome 17 and mouse chromosome 11.
source: First, they are located at a syntenic region on human chromosome 17 and mouse chromosome 11.
evidence: Supported by genomic location analysis.

claim: Human FORCP and its mouse homolog have well-conserved 240 nt ORFs that have the potential to be translated into a 79 amino acid small protein.
source: Second, they have well-conserved 240 nt ORFs that have the potential to be translated into a 79 amino acid small protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by sequence comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The mouse homolog of FORCP shows biased expression in the GI-tract, similar to human FORCP.
source: Third, similar to the human FORCP, the mouse homolog shows biased expression in the GI-tract (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by mouse ENCODE transcriptome data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Mass spectrometry from SW1222 whole cell lysates identified an N-terminal peptide MLLGSLWGR that is unique to the FORCP protein.
source: To determine if the FORCP RNA is translated into an endogenously expressed protein, we performed mass spectrometry analysis from SW1222 whole cell lysates. We identified an N-terminal peptide MLLGSLWGR that was unique to the FORCP protein (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A rabbit polyclonal antibody against FORCP detects endogenous FORCP in SW1222 whole cell lysates that co-migrates with untagged FORCP protein overexpressed in 293T cells.
source: We therefore generated a rabbit polyclonal antibody against the FORCP protein. This antibody detected endogenous FORCP in SW1222 whole cell lysates that co-migrated with untagged FORCP protein overexpressed in 293T cells transduced with a lentivirus (pLVX-FORCP) (Figure 2D and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Knockdown of FORCP in SW1222 abolishes expression of the FORCP protein.
source: Knockdown of FORCP in SW1222 abolished expression of the FORCP protein (Figure 2E and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data after FORCP knockdown shown in Figure 2E.

claim: FORCP is a novel protein-coding gene and not a lncRNA.
source: These data indicate that FORCP is a novel protein-coding gene and not a lncRNA.
evidence: Inferred from mass spectrometry identification of FORCP peptide and antibody detection of endogenous FORCP protein.

claim: The FORCP-FLAG protein is expressed only in pLVX-WT FORCP transduced cells and not in cells transduced with mutant FORCP where the start codon ATG was mutated to ATT.
source: To test this, we overexpressed wild-type (WT) FORCP full-length RNA or a FORCP mutant in which the start codon ATG was mutated to ATT and inserted three copies of the FLAG-tag before the stop codon. As expected, the FORCP-FLAG protein was expressed only in the pLVX-WT FORCP transduced cells (Figure 2F and Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The expression levels of WT and Mutant FORCP RNAs are comparable.
source: At the RNA level, the expression levels of the WT and Mutant FORCP RNAs were comparable (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Overexpression of FORCP-WT but not mutant FORCP in HCT116 results in significant growth defects as measured by cell proliferation assays.
source: Overexpression of FORCP-WT but not the mutant FORCP in HCT116 resulted in significant growth defects as measured by cell proliferation assays (Figure 2G)
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Overexpression of FORCP-WT but not mutant FORCP in HCT116 inhibits colony formation on plastic and soft agar.
source: colony formation assays on plastic and soft agar colony formation assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and C)
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: Exogenous FORCP inhibits proliferation as a protein-coding gene.
source: indicating that exogenous FORCP inhibits proliferation as a protein-coding gene.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that only WT FORCP (which produces protein) but not mutant FORCP (which does not produce protein) inhibits proliferation despite comparable RNA levels.

claim: FORCP-GFP fusion protein is predominantly localized to the ER, colocalizing with the ER marker PDI.
source: Unlike GFP which was localized to the nucleus and cytoplasm, FORCP-GFP was predominantly localized to the ER, colocalizing with the ER marker PDI (protein disulfide isomerase) (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data showing colocalization with PDI shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: A small fraction of FORCP-GFP is found in the perinuclear region.
source: However, a small fraction of FORCP-GFP was also found in the perinuclear region.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy observations.

claim: FORCP could be a double-pass transmembrane protein with two transmembrane helices.
source: Further analysis using the TMHMM Server v. 2.0 indicated that FORCP could be a double-pass transmembrane protein with two transmembrane helices
evidence: Supported by TMHMM Server v. 2.0 analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The C-terminus of the FORCP protein is homologous to TMEM238, a transmembrane protein.
source: and BLASTX analysis revealed that the C-terminus of the FORCP protein is homologous to TMEM238, a transmembrane protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by BLASTX analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Endogenous FORCP is localized to the ER in LS180 cells.
source: To determine if the endogenous FORCP protein resides in the ER, we assayed for its localization using the anti-FORCP antibody. In LS180, we observed cytoplasmic ER-like staining of the FORCP protein that was strongly reduced upon knockdown of FORCP with siRNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A). Colocalization experiments with PDI suggested that endogenous FORCP is localized to the ER (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and colocalization data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Knockdown of FORCP in SW1222 results in increased proliferation.
source: Knockdown of FORCP in SW1222 resulted in increased proliferation (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by Incucyte live cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Knockdown of FORCP in SW1222 results in increased clonogenic potential on plastic.
source: increased clonogenic potential on plastic (Figure 3E and F)
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Knockdown of FORCP in SW1222 results in increased colony formation on soft agar.
source: and increased colony formation on soft agar, a measure of tumorigenicity in vitro (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by soft agar colony formation assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: FORCP knockdown in SW1222 results in enhanced tumor growth in mouse xenografts.
source: In concordance with these data, we observed enhanced tumor growth in mouse xenografts upon FORCP knockdown in SW1222 (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by mouse xenograft data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: FORCP functions to inhibit proliferation and could suppress tumorigenicity.
source: These data suggest that FORCP functions to inhibit proliferation and could suppress tumorigenicity.
evidence: Inferred from increased proliferation, clonogenicity, and tumor growth upon FORCP knockdown.

claim: FORCP is upregulated approximately 3-4 fold upon treatment of LS180 with the ER-stress inducers DTT or tunicamycin.
source: When we measured FORCP levels upon treatment of LS180 with the ER-stress inducers dithiothreitol (DTT) or tunicamycin (TM), we found that FORCP was upregulated ~3–4 fold (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data after ER stress induction shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Upregulation of FORCP upon ER stress in FOXA1 knockdown cells is less marked, perhaps due to a decrease in basal FORCP levels.
source: Interestingly, unlike basal FORCP expression which was controlled by FOXA1, upregulation of FORCP upon ER stress in FOXA1 knockdown cells was less marked, perhaps due to a decrease in basal FORCP levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data after FOXA1 knockdown and ER stress shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Upon ER stress, silencing FORCP using siRNAs results in significantly better survival as assessed by cell viability and colony formation assays.
source: Upon ER stress, silencing FORCP using siRNAs resulted in significantly better survival as compared to the control as assessed by cell viability and colony formation assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: Supported by cell viability and colony formation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: The improved cell viability upon FORCP knockdown during ER stress is due to a decrease in apoptosis as measured by the sub-G1 population in LS180.
source: The improved cell viability upon FORCP knockdown during ER stress was due to a decrease in apoptosis as measured by the sub-G1 population in LS180 (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: Supported by PI staining and FACS analysis data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The improved cell viability upon FORCP knockdown during ER stress is due to a decrease in apoptosis in SW1222.
source: and SW1222 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by PI staining and FACS analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The pro-apoptotic effect of FORCP is confirmed by immunoblotting for the apoptosis marker cleaved caspase-3.
source: The pro-apoptotic effect of FORCP was further confirmed by immunoblotting for the apoptosis marker cleaved caspase-3 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data for cleaved caspase-3 shown in Figure 4B.

claim: FORCP-KO LS180 cells show decreased apoptosis in response to ER stress compared to FORCP-WT cells.
source: As compared to FORCP-WT cells, FORCP-KO cells showed significant reduction in FORCP expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B) and decreased apoptosis in response to ER stress (Figure 4C and D, and Figure 4—source data 2), further establishing a pro-apoptotic role of FORCP during ER stress.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting for cleaved caspase-3 and PI staining/FACS analysis shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: FORCP-KO cells display increased basal proliferation and clonogenicity compared to FORCP-WT cells.
source: In addition, the FORCP-KO cells displayed increased basal proliferation and clonogenicity as compared to FORCP-WT cells, further supporting our data from the FORCP knockdown experiments (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by colony formation and cell count assay data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: In response to glucose deprivation induced by 2-DG, FORCP-KO cells display a modest but significantly improved viability compared to FORCP-WT cells.
source: Finally, in response to another stress, namely glucose deprivation induced by treating the cells with 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG), the FORCP-KO cells displayed a modest but significantly improved viability as compared to FORCP-WT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data after 2-DG treatment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Sixteen FORCP-FLAG-interacting proteins were enriched in all four pulldown experiments.
source: We found 16 FORCP-FLAG-interacting proteins enriched in all four pulldowns (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data from four biological replicates of anti-FLAG pulldowns.

claim: Seven of the sixteen FORCP-FLAG-interacting proteins appeared in less than 30 of the 411 experiments in the CRAPOME dataset.
source: Of these 16 proteins, seven appeared in less than 30 of the 411 experiments in the CRAPOME dataset (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by comparison with CRAPOME database shown in Figure 4G.

claim: FORCP-FLAG interacts with BRI3BP as validated by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: We next validated the interaction between FORCP-FLAG and BRI3BP by co-transfecting 293 T cells with constructs expressing FORCP-FLAG and BRI3BP-FLAG-Myc followed by anti-Myc IP and immunoblotting using an anti-FLAG antibody (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Knockdown of BRI3BP results in significantly increased apoptosis when ER stress is induced using DTT.
source: Unlike FORCP, knockdown of BRI3BP resulted in significantly increased apoptosis when ER stress was induced using DTT (Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by PI staining and FACS analysis data after BRI3BP knockdown and DTT treatment shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: FORCP could inhibit BRI3BP function or vice versa in the context of ER stress.
source: These data on the FORCP-BRI3BP interaction raise the possibility that FORCP could inhibit BRI3BP function or vice versa in the context of ER stress.
evidence: Speculated based on the opposite effects of FORCP and BRI3BP knockdown on apoptosis during ER stress.

claim: FORCP is a novel protein-coding gene that was mis-annotated as a lncRNA.
source: Here, we report the identification and initial characterization of FORCP as a novel, highly conserved, small protein expressed from a transcript annotated as a lncRNA (LINC00675).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry identification of FORCP peptide, antibody detection of endogenous protein, and functional studies showing protein-dependent effects.

claim: FORCP is an ER-localized protein that is robustly expressed in well-differentiated CRC cells.
source: Our data demonstrate that FORCP is an ER-localized protein that is robustly expressed in well-differentiated CRC cells and that FOXA1 controls its transcription.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy showing ER localization and RNA-seq showing expression in well-differentiated CRC cells.

claim: FOXA1 controls FORCP transcription.
source: Our data demonstrate that FORCP is an ER-localized protein that is robustly expressed in well-differentiated CRC cells and that FOXA1 controls its transcription.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq showing FOXA1 binding to FORCP locus and decreased FORCP expression upon FOXA1 knockdown.

claim: FORCP inhibits proliferation at the basal level.
source: Functionally, we found that FORCP inhibits proliferation at the basal level
evidence: Supported by increased proliferation and clonogenicity upon FORCP knockdown or knockout.

claim: FORCP is pro-apoptotic in the context of ER stress.
source: and is pro-apoptotic in the context of ER stress.
evidence: Supported by decreased apoptosis upon FORCP knockdown or knockout during ER stress.

claim: FORCP is mis-annotated as a lncRNA in contrast to current annotations and publications.
source: In contrast to current annotations and publications on this gene (Li et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2018; Zhong et al., 2018; Shan et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018), we found that FORCP is mis-annotated as a lncRNA.
evidence: Supported by experimental evidence showing FORCP encodes a functional protein, contradicting previous annotations.

claim: Short ORFs are often hidden in lncRNAs and are translated into small proteins or micropeptides that play essential roles in regulation of fundamental biological processes in organisms ranging from bacteria to humans.
source: Our discovery that FORCP is translated into a small protein contributes to the emerging notion that short ORFs are often hidden in lncRNAs and are translated into small proteins or micropeptides that play essential roles in regulation of fundamental biological processes in organisms ranging from bacteria to humans (Hartford and Lal, 2020; Makarewich and Olson, 2017; Storz et al., 2014; Leslie, 2019; Orr et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on small proteins encoded by lncRNAs.

claim: The small size of micropeptides can allow them to block or boost the activity of the larger proteins they interact with.
source: Although the exact molecular mechanisms by which these small proteins mediate their effects remains largely unclear, there is some evidence that the small size of these proteins can allow them to block or boost the activity of the larger proteins they interact with (Leslie, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The micropeptide MOXI localizes to the inner mitochondrial membrane where it interacts with mitochondrial trifunctional protein.
source: For example, the micropeptide MOXI localizes to the inner mitochondrial membrane where it interacts with mitochondrial trifunctional protein (Makarewich et al., 2018b)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The micropeptide DWORF localizes to the sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle cells where it enhances SERCA activity by displacing the SERCA inhibitors phospholamban, sarcolipin, and myoregulin.
source: whereas the micropeptide DWORF localizes to the sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle cells where it enhances SERCA activity by displacing the SERCA inhibitors phospholamban, sarcolipin, and myoregulin (Nelson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: FORCP was not expressed in the commonly used CRC cell lines and in 57 cell lines in the NCI-60 panel.
source: Surprisingly, FORCP was not expressed in the commonly used CRC cell lines and in 57 cell lines in the NCI-60 panel.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from NCI-60 panel shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: FORCP is abundant in well-differentiated CRC cells that are colon-like, consistent with high FORCP expression in normal human colon tissue.
source: FORCP was abundant in well-differentiated CRC cells that are colon-like, consistent with high FORCP expression in the normal human colon tissue.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing FORCP expression in well-differentiated CRC cells and normal colon tissue.

claim: Identifying the appropriate cell type was instrumental in the discovery of the FORCP protein, identification of FOXA1 as an upstream regulator of FORCP and for functional analysis.
source: Identifying the appropriate cell type was instrumental in the discovery of the FORCP protein, identification of FOXA1 as an upstream regulator of FORCP and for functional analysis.
evidence: Inferred from the fact that FORCP was only detectable in well-differentiated CRC cells, which enabled all subsequent discoveries.

claim: The discovery of FORCP as a novel protein-coding gene, together with recent reports on other lncRNA-encoded small proteins, reveals vital functions of small proteins translated from ORFs hidden in lncRNAs.
source: In summary, the discovery of FORCP as a novel protein-coding gene, together with recent reports on other lncRNA-encoded small proteins, reveals vital functions of small proteins translated from ORFs hidden in lncRNAs
evidence: Supported by the functional characterization of FORCP and citations to other studies on lncRNA-encoded proteins.

claim: There is a need to determine the coding potential of cytoplasmic lncRNAs in an endogenous setting.
source: and underscores the need to determine the coding potential of cytoplasmic lncRNAs in an endogenous setting.
evidence: Inferred from the discovery that FORCP, annotated as a lncRNA, actually encodes a functional protein.

claim: Future studies will likely identify new mis-annotated lncRNAs that encode functional small proteins important for normal development and human diseases.
source: Future studies will likely identify new mis-annotated lncRNAs that encode functional small proteins important for normal development and human diseases.
evidence: Speculated based on the discovery of FORCP and the large number of uncharacterized lncRNAs.

claim: KDSR and CERS2 were identified as FORCP-interacting proteins.
source: Given that we identified KDSR and CERS2 as FORCP-interacting proteins
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data from FORCP-FLAG pulldowns shown in Figure 4G.

claim: KDSR and CERS2 catalyze sequential steps in ceramide biosynthesis.
source: and that these proteins catalyze sequential steps in ceramide biosynthesis
evidence: Based on established knowledge about KDSR and CERS2 function.

claim: FORCP may have a role in ceramide biosynthesis.
source: it would be interesting to determine if FORCP has a role in ceramide biosynthesis.
evidence: Speculated based on the interaction of FORCP with KDSR and CERS2, which are involved in ceramide biosynthesis.

claim: BRI3BP was reported in a subnetwork of proteins important for ER biology.
source: Of these seven proteins, we focused on BRI3BP (BRI3-binding protein) because it had been reported in a subnetwork of proteins important for ER biology (Christianson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) are often associated with polysomes, indicating coding potential.
source: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) are often associated with polysomes, indicating coding potential.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about lncRNA-ribosome associations.

claim: Only a handful of endogenous proteins encoded by putative lncRNAs have been identified and assigned a function.
source: However, only a handful of endogenous proteins encoded by putative lncRNAs have been identified and assigned a function.
evidence: Based on the state of knowledge in the field at the time of publication.

claim: LINC00675 is a putative gastrointestinal-tract-specific lncRNA.
source: Here, we report the discovery of a putative gastrointestinal-tract-specific lncRNA (LINC00675)
evidence: Supported by expression data showing GI-tract-specific expression.

claim: LINC00675 is regulated by the pioneer transcription factor FOXA1.
source: that is regulated by the pioneer transcription factor FOXA1
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and knockdown experiments showing FOXA1 regulation of FORCP.

claim: LINC00675 encodes a conserved small protein of 79 amino acids termed FORCP (FOXA1-Regulated Conserved Small Protein).
source: and encodes a conserved small protein of 79 amino acids which we termed FORCP (FOXA1-Regulated Conserved Small Protein).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry identification of FORCP peptide and sequence analysis showing conservation.

claim: FORCP transcript is undetectable in most cell types but is abundant in well-differentiated colorectal cancer (CRC) cells.
source: FORCP transcript is undetectable in most cell types but is abundant in well-differentiated colorectal cancer (CRC) cells
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from NCI-60 panel and CRC cell lines.

claim: FORCP functions to inhibit proliferation, clonogenicity, and tumorigenesis in well-differentiated CRC cells.
source: where it functions to inhibit proliferation, clonogenicity, and tumorigenesis.
evidence: Supported by proliferation assays, colony formation assays, and mouse xenograft experiments.

claim: The epitope-tagged and endogenous FORCP protein predominantly localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: The epitope-tagged and endogenous FORCP protein predominantly localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy showing colocalization with ER marker PDI.

claim: In response to ER stress, FORCP depletion results in decreased apoptosis.
source: In response to ER stress, FORCP depletion results in decreased apoptosis.
evidence: Supported by PI staining/FACS analysis and cleaved caspase-3 immunoblotting after FORCP knockdown during ER stress.

claim: FORCP is a novel, conserved small protein encoded by a mis-annotated lncRNA that regulates apoptosis and tumorigenicity in well-differentiated CRC cells.
source: Our findings on the initial characterization of FORCP demonstrate that FORCP is a novel, conserved small protein encoded by a mis-annotated lncRNA that regulates apoptosis and tumorigenicity in well-differentiated CRC cells.
evidence: Supported by the comprehensive characterization of FORCP including protein identification, functional assays, and localization studies.

claim: The human genome harbors thousands of long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) genes transcribed into a heterogeneous group of transcripts > 200 nucleotides (nt) long.
source: The human genome harbors thousands of long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) genes transcribed into a heterogeneous group of transcripts > 200 nucleotides (nt) long (Harrow et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The vast majority of lncRNAs have not been functionally characterized.
source: Although the vast majority of lncRNAs have not been functionally characterized
evidence: Based on the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Some lncRNAs have established functions in development and disease.
source: some have established functions in development and disease (Fatica and Bozzoni, 2014; Li and Chang, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: lncRNAs control diverse cellular processes including dosage compensation, differentiation, proliferation, apoptosis, metastasis, DNA repair, and genome stability maintenance.
source: and control diverse cellular processes including dosage compensation, differentiation, proliferation, apoptosis, metastasis, DNA repair, and genome stability maintenance (Fatica and Bozzoni, 2014; Lee et al., 2016; Munschauer et al., 2018; Sharma et al., 2015; Arun et al., 2016; Sahakyan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: lncRNA expression is frequently altered in cancer.
source: lncRNA expression is frequently altered in cancer (Prensner and Chinnaiyan, 2011; Huarte and Rinn, 2010; Huarte, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some lncRNAs play important roles in mediating the effects of tumor-suppressive transcription factors such as p53.
source: We and others have shown that some lncRNAs play important roles in mediating the effects of tumor-suppressive transcription factors such as p53 (Chaudhary et al., 2017; Li et al., 2017; Adriaens et al., 2016; Hünten et al., 2015; Léveillé et al., 2015; Grossi et al., 2016; Marín-Béjar et al., 2017; Huarte et al., 2010; Chaudhary and Lal, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature including authors' own work.

claim: Unlike mRNAs that are predominantly cytoplasmic, lncRNAs can be nuclear and/or cytoplasmic.
source: Unlike mRNAs that are predominantly cytoplasmic, lncRNAs can be nuclear and/or cytoplasmic (Cabili et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Nuclear lncRNAs are bona fide noncoding.
source: While nuclear lncRNAs are bona fide noncoding
evidence: Based on established knowledge that nuclear localization prevents translation.

claim: Cytoplasmic lncRNAs have the potential to be translated if they interact with ribosomes.
source: cytoplasmic lncRNAs have the potential to be translated if they interact with ribosomes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about translation mechanisms.

claim: Hundreds of cytoplasmic lncRNAs, harboring evolutionary conserved open-reading frames (ORFs) are associated with ribosomes.
source: Indeed, hundreds of cytoplasmic lncRNAs, harboring evolutionary conserved open-reading frames (ORFs) are associated with ribosomes (Carlevaro-Fita et al., 2016; Ingolia et al., 2014; Ingolia et al., 2011; Hartford and Lal, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature including ribosome profiling studies.

claim: Small proteins derived from mis-annotated lncRNAs have vital functions in many organisms ranging from bacteria to humans.
source: and small proteins derived from such mis-annotated lncRNAs have vital functions in many organisms ranging from bacteria to humans (Makarewich and Olson, 2017; Storz et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Small proteins encoded by lncRNAs regulate diverse processes including stress response.
source: These small proteins regulate diverse processes including stress response (Slavoff et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Small proteins encoded by lncRNAs regulate development.
source: development (Chng et al., 2013; Kondo et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Small proteins encoded by lncRNAs regulate calcium homeostasis.
source: calcium homeostasis (Anderson et al., 2015)
